items.headline: Want to Referee? Start at the Club
items.body:
USA Fencing's advice for would-be referees starts small: at your own club, when two fencers are bouting, offer to referee. Practice every chance you get, ideally with an experienced referee or a coach as a mentor, and read the rulebook. Even if you never ref a tournament, USA Fencing says, knowing the rules makes you a better fencer, one who can speak up when a rule is misapplied.

Certification comes in steps. Download the Referee Study Guide, take a referee seminar, then take the online exam: a general section plus at least one weapon section, and you need 90 percent on each. There's a fee, and a failed exam can be retaken within 48 hours. Pass, and you hold a P rating.

After that, ratings are earned on the strip. A practical exam from a Referee Examiner is the step to a local or regional rating, and the ladder runs from L2 and L1 (local events) to R2 and R1 (regional) and N2 and N1 (national). Examiners look for consistency: the same call at 14-14 as at 1-1.

You don't have to be an adult. Referees as young as 13 with a P rating may work regional tournaments, and at those events anyone who referees more than a single round of pools must be paid. Every referee needs a current USA Fencing membership; referees 18 and older also need a background check and SafeSport training. To keep a rating, retake the exam every two years, attend a seminar, and referee at your level at least once every two years.

Friday open bouting at Elite FC is a good place to start.

items.headline: Winter Camp: Sign Up Now
items.body: Elite FC Winter Camp runs Dec. 27–31, 9:30 a.m. to 2 p.m., and it's open to all levels: footwork, technical and tactical drills, and games. Dec. 27 starts with a swag giveaway. K2 Fitness runs strength and conditioning on Dec. 28 and 30. On Dec. 29, a professional instructor leads yoga and breath control for competition, and lunch is served. Crepes on Dec. 31 celebrate the end of camp and 2026. Call it a tune-up for the second half of the season, or a good excuse to escape visiting relatives for a few hours. If you're going, let the club know as soon as possible for a headcount; contact the club for price and sign-up.

items.headline: Italy, Hungary Win Epee Season Opener
items.body: The senior epee World Cup season opened in Casablanca, Morocco, Oct. 15–18, with 618 fencers from 67 nations. Italy's Roberta Marzani won the women's event, with Ukraine's Anna Maksymenko second and Aizanat Murtazaeva (Russia) and Alberta Santuccio (Italy) third. Hungary's Mate Tamas Koch won the men's title over Italy's Matteo Galassi; Gergely Kovacs (Hungary) and Kano Koki (Japan) took bronze. In the team events, Kazakhstan's men beat Russia 45-40, and Russia's women edged Italy 32-31. The next senior epee World Cups are Berne (men) and Wuxi (women), Nov. 12–15.

items.headline: By the Book: One Quiet Minute
items.body: In a direct-elimination bout, a full minute of fencing with no touch is "unwillingness to fight" (t.124), and the referee calls "Halt!" The first time, both fencers get a P-red card, a penalty hit. The second time, the fencer who is behind gets a P-black card and loses the bout; if the score is tied, the lower seed gets it. The minute restarts after every touch and at the start of each period, and no P-card can be given at 14-14 (or 9-9 in a 10-touch bout).
items.vetted_by: standing rule (Frank voice 2026-10-18: Desk-written By the Book goes in; approve or cut at budget)

facts.claim: One minute of fencing without a hit (or off-target hit) = unwillingness to fight; referee calls Halt as a decision of fact
facts.citation: t.124 (USA Fencing Rules for Competition, Oct 2026, p.47-48)

facts.claim: Individual DE: first time, P-red to both fencers simultaneously
Second time: P-black to the lower score (higher score wins); if equal, P-black to the lower initial seeding (higher seed wins)
P-red = penalty hit; P-black = possible loss of the bout
No P-card at 14-14; in USA Fencing competitions, none at 9-9 in 10-touch bouts
The minute restarts after each hit, off-target hit, annulled hit, penalty hit, and at the start of each period

items.headline: For the Parents: The Time Listed Is Check-In
items.body: On a tournament schedule, the time next to an event is often when check-in closes, not when fencing starts. The Ultimate Cup page says it outright: "All times are Close of Check-in," and organizers recommend arriving at least an hour before. Fencers check in every day they compete. Equipment check opens the Friday before, 4 to 6:30 p.m., and from 6:30 a.m. on event days. Spectators sit outside the barriers around the strips.

items.headline: Photo from History: 1976: The light came on, but there was no touch
items.body: During the epee round of the 1976 Olympic modern pentathlon, British competitors challenged touches credited to Boris Onishchenko. In his bout with Jim Fox, the scoring light registered a hit even though his weapon had not reached its target. Examination revealed deliberate tampering that allowed the epee to signal a touch without contact. Onishchenko was disqualified, ending the Soviet team’s medal chances, although his teammates could continue individually. Britain went on to win team gold. The incident occurred in modern pentathlon, not the separate Olympic fencing tournament. The accompanying 2006 equipment photograph shows a normal electric epee, not the weapon involved.
items.caption: At Montreal in 1976, Boris Onishchenko was disqualified from modern pentathlon after officials found that his epee could register touches without hitting an opponent. This 2006 photograph shows an ordinary electric epee grip and connector, not Onishchenko’s weapon.
items.credit: Illustrative equipment photo: Lord ignus, “Pistolgrip.jpg” (25 May 2006), via Wikimedia Commons. Public domain by the photographer. Not Onishchenko’s weapon. Release: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Pistolgrip.jpg#Licensing. Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Pistolgrip.jpg.
items.alt_text: Color close-up of a normal electric epee on a wooden surface, showing a gray pistol grip inside a metal bell guard, a red pad and a three-socket connector.
